public_summary: Jungle Chess played with the solar system. Every piece is a planet, and a planet's size on the board is the fifth root of its real measured diameter, so rank is something you can see rather than learn: Mercury is the smallest world in play and Jupiter the largest, and the traditional rules are followed exactly as written. Matter faces antimatter. One army's worlds lean their poles one way and the other army's lean the other, by each planet's own true axial tilt, and the bases say it again in white against black. Four of the eight wear a real map -- Earth its coastlines, Mars its dark continents, Mercury its smooth plains with the Caloris basin in them, and Venus the radar surface no eye has seen. Three more wear their weather. One wears nothing at all. This edition changes one thing on one world: Neptune's Great Dark Spot gets the bright companion cloud that sits just south of it, on both armies -- one small white oval, ten degrees of arc long and five tall, on the spot's own meridian. The set knew it was missing. An earlier edition drew it, a later one reverted the cloud marking it lived inside and took it along without meaning to, and the design contract recorded the loss as a live recommendation. This edition settles it, and gives it a marking key of its own so the next argument about bands cannot take it again. It is not free: on a spot fourteen degrees tall, a cloud five degrees tall centred eight degrees below its centre overlaps the rim, so the spot is cut back to leave a printable strip of blue between them and now carries a shallow bay on its southern edge. That trade is stated in full in the limitations. No printed part changes: both Neptune pieces come out of the generator byte-for-byte identical to the last edition's, and the whole change lives in which spool prints which part of them.
